before: After a car accident, one of the first questions people ask is: "Who got the ticket?" Traffic citations issued at an accident scene can play an important role in your injury claim — but they do not automatically determine fault. Understanding how traffic tickets interact with personal injury claims in Georgia and South Carolina is crucial for protecting your right to compensation. For a comprehensive overview of car accident claims, visit our car accident lawyers page. According to the Cornell Law Institute's overview of negligence per se, violating a traffic statute can serve as evidence of negligence in a civil lawsuit, though the relationship between traffic citations and civil liability is more nuanced than most people realize.
after: After a car accident, one of the first questions people ask is: "Who got the ticket?" Understanding how traffic tickets interact with personal injury claims in Georgia and South Carolina is crucial for protecting your right to compensation. According to the Legal Information Institute at Cornell Law School, violating a traffic statute can serve as evidence of negligence in a civil lawsuit, though the relationship between traffic citations and civil liability is more nuanced than most people realize.

before:
A traffic ticket is strong evidence of fault but is not the final word. In both Georgia and South Carolina, fault in a car accident is determined by the civil legal system — not by the police officer who issued the citation. A traffic ticket reflects the officer's assessment of who violated traffic laws, but it is just one piece of evidence in a broader fault analysis. Here is why traffic tickets are not conclusive on the question of fault:
  • The officer may not have witnessed the accident — they are reconstructing events from evidence and witness statements
  • Traffic court and civil court have different standards of proof
  • A driver can receive a ticket but still not be primarily at fault for the collision
  • Both drivers can receive citations, creating shared fault scenarios
  • A ticket can be dismissed in traffic court but still be referenced in a civil claim
That said, a traffic citation — especially for a serious violation like running a red light or DUI — carries significant weight in settlement negotiations and at trial. Insurance adjusters and juries both view traffic tickets as meaningful indicators of fault.
after:
A traffic ticket carries real weight with insurance adjusters, but it is not the final word. In both Georgia and South Carolina, fault in a car accident is determined by the civil legal system — not by the police officer who issued the citation. A traffic ticket reflects the officer's assessment of who violated traffic laws, but in both states the ticket itself is generally not even admissible at trial; the jury decides fault from the evidence of what each driver did. Here is why traffic tickets are not conclusive on the question of fault:
  • The officer may not have witnessed the accident — they are reconstructing events from evidence and witness statements
  • Traffic court and civil court have different standards of proof
  • A driver can receive a ticket but still not be primarily at fault for the collision
  • Both drivers can receive citations, creating shared fault scenarios
  • A ticket can be dismissed in traffic court and the underlying conduct can still be proven in the civil case with witnesses and physical evidence
That said, a traffic citation — especially for a serious violation like running a red light or DUI — carries significant weight in settlement negotiations, and a guilty plea to it can be used against the driver at trial. Insurance adjusters treat citations as meaningful indicators of fault.

before: In Georgia, a traffic citation issued at the scene of an accident is generally admissible as evidence in a civil lawsuit. The citation itself does not prove fault conclusively, but it can be presented to the jury as evidence supporting a negligence claim. If the at-fault driver pleaded guilty to or was convicted of the traffic violation, that outcome strengthens the negligence per se argument significantly.
after: In Georgia, the traffic citation itself is generally not admissible in a civil lawsuit: courts have consistently held that a traffic-court charge or its disposition is inadmissible unless the driver pleaded guilty (Eubanks v. Waldron). A guilty plea, or posting a cash bond and not appearing, which O.C.G.A. § 40-13-58 treats as an admission of guilt, makes a prima facie showing of negligence the driver must then rebut (Coleman v. Fortner). Merely paying a fine is not by itself an admission, a conviction after a contested traffic trial is not admissible, and a plea of nolo contendere can never be used (O.C.G.A. § 17-7-95(c)).

Traffic citations play a similar evidentiary role in South Carolina civil cases. after: South Carolina also follows a modified comparative fault system that allows recovery as long as you are less than 51% at fault. before: South Carolina courts allow traffic citations to be admitted as evidence in personal injury cases. A conviction on the underlying traffic charge — especially for violations like DUI (S.C. Code § 56-5-2930), reckless driving, or failure to yield — provides strong support for a negligence per se claim. However, South Carolina courts have also held that the absence of a citation does not mean the absence of fault.
after: By statute, no evidence of a traffic conviction is admissible in any civil action (S.C. Code § 56-5-6160), and the investigating officer may testify to observations, not to an opinion on who caused the crash, unless qualified as an expert (Gulledge v. McLaughlin). What can come in is a guilty plea, which courts treat as an admission the driver may explain or rebut; a bond forfeiture or a plea of nolo contendere cannot be used as an admission (Samuel v. Mouzon), even though S.C. Code § 56-5-6220 gives both the effect of a conviction for traffic-law purposes. Proving the violation itself — DUI (S.C. Code § 56-5-2930), reckless driving (S.C. Code § 56-5-2920), or failure to yield — is what supports a negligence per se claim. And the absence of a citation does not mean the absence of fault.

before: Under South Carolina's comparative fault system, traffic violations by both drivers are weighed against each other. If both drivers received citations, the jury determines each party's percentage of fault based on the severity of the violations and their causal connection to the accident.
after: Under South Carolina's comparative fault system, traffic violations by both drivers are weighed against each other. If both drivers were cited, the jury still decides each party's percentage of fault from the evidence of what each driver did and how much it contributed to the crash, not from the citations, which it will not see.

  • Settlement negotiations — insurance adjusters review traffic citations when evaluating fault and determining settlement offers
  • Depositions — attorneys may question the cited driver about the violation and whether they contested it

This is why the decision to plead guilty to a traffic ticket after an accident should never be taken lightly. What seems like a simple way to pay a fine and move on can significantly impact your personal injury case — whether you are the one pursuing a claim or defending against one.
after:
• Police report — the accident report documents which citations were issued and typically includes the officer's narrative of how the accident occurred; adjusters lean on it, but in South Carolina it may not be used as evidence of either party's negligence at trial (S.C. Code § 56-5-1290)
  • Settlement negotiations — insurance adjusters review traffic citations when evaluating fault and determining settlement offers
  • Depositions — attorneys may question the cited driver about the violation and whether they contested it
  • Trial evidence — the officer's testimony about what he or she observed, and any guilty plea, can be presented to a jury; the citation itself and a traffic-court conviction generally cannot
  • Guilty pleas — if the cited driver pleaded guilty to the traffic violation, that admission is powerful evidence of fault in a civil case
This is why the decision to plead guilty to a traffic ticket after an accident should never be taken lightly. In Georgia, a driver who posts a cash bond and skips traffic court is treated as having admitted guilt (O.C.G.A. § 40-13-58); South Carolina will not admit a forfeited bond, but it will admit a guilty plea. In both states a plea of nolo contendere, where the court allows it, is not an admission.

before: Negligence per se is a legal doctrine where violating a safety statute — such as a traffic law — is automatically considered negligent. For it to apply, the violation must have been the proximate cause of the accident. A citation for running a red light that caused a collision supports negligence per se; a broken taillight citation in a head-on collision does not.
after: Negligence per se is a legal doctrine under which violating a safety statute — such as a traffic law — establishes that the driver breached a duty of care, so the injured person does not have to prove separately that the driver acted unreasonably. It applies only when the injured person is within the group the statute protects and the harm is the kind it was meant to prevent, and the violation must still be shown to be the proximate cause of the accident. Running a red light that caused a collision supports negligence per se; a broken taillight in a head-on collision does not.
